I have the smallest available Instant Pot. Not sure what size it is, but it's very small, capacity-wise. I was able to fit a large yellow onion, half a large russet potato, a can of diced tomatoes, a bay leaf, some chopped parsley, and three frozen boneless skinless chicken thighs in the pot. It came up to just under the max fill line. Despite using an objectively inferior chicken product, it still came out perfect, so if you're not into soggy chicken skin or navigating bones in a dish you'd otherwise eat with a spoon, you can totally use boneless skinless chicken and still get good results. The texture won't be the same, but that's the price of convenience. I will say if you go this route you must use chicken thighs, since breasts would almost certainly dry out from fifteen minutes at high pressure. If you don't have a tomato garden or it's winter, canned tomatoes are terrific. That said, I didn't care for all the seeds I bit into, so next time I might go for tomato sauce or try to de-seed whole canned tomatoes. It wasn't a huge deal, though, and I get that this dish is supposed to be rustic. As for the onion, I was worried that a whole onion would be too much for this capacity, but the pieces gave off a ton of water and shrank down to almost nothing, and there wasn't an overwhelming onion flavor. Lastly, I think in the future I'd use a waxier potato, like a red variety. Russets are fine, but they do get really soft when cooked like this, so I think a red potato would give better texture and probably survive at a smaller dice. This is of course my opinion, so pick your favorite stewing potato.

Overall this feels like such an easily adaptable recipe. I added some fresh parsley that I had from another recipe, but you could add all sorts of herbs and spices to this, or even add other vegetables. For example, I bet adobo seasoning and a parsnip would be lovely in this. I've seen others talk about using tomatillos and peppers, which would also be fantastic. I bet you could even use a different meat if you researched cooking times. This is such a versatile technique that you can easily adapt it into an entirely different set of ingredients.
